implementation_notes: serde derives the mapper: #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] plus serde_json::to_vec/from_slice turns the graph into JSON/JSONB bytes, and sqlx's Json<T> wrapper binds and decodes the column so no hand-written serializer survives. Ownership makes the round trip explicit - the column yields owned data that can only be borrowed within its scope - and unknown-field handling is opted into per type with serde attributes.
pitfalls: serde ignores unknown fields by default, so without #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] a renamed field silently loses data on the next rewrite.
sqlx's Json<T> decodes through serde_json, which allocates proportionally to the input: bound the payload size when stored blobs are not fully trusted.
Derived forms follow the field names in the struct; renaming a Rust field without a serde rename breaks compatibility with rows written by the previous release.

variants.name: bincode/postcard binary blob
variants.idiom_name: serde binary format into a BYTEA/BLOB column
variants.implementation_notes: The same serde derives feed a binary format such as bincode or postcard, which writes the graph compactly into a BYTEA/BLOB column with no field names on the wire. Choose it when payload size or decode speed matters and the data stays inside one deployment; the format is not self-describing, so versioning is entirely the application's responsibility.
pitfalls: Non-self-describing formats cannot encode #[serde(flatten)] or untagged enums, so a graph that uses them must stay on JSON.
Field order and enum tags are implicit in the format: any struct change silently corrupts decoding unless an explicit format version gates the reader.
